articles.title: Eighth annual Indigenous Peoples' Day powwow
articles.description: On Indigenous Peoples' Day, Monday, Oct. 12 the Center for Diversity & Inclusion's department of Multicultural Affairs hosted its eighth annual powwow celebration inside the Levering Glass Pavilion. A powwow is a traditional social gathering of Indigenous people containing dancing and singing. The event began with remarks from Mary Rose Pedron, the associate director of Multicultural Affairs, and Sherry Ayers, a member of the Lumbee Tribe and former commissioner of the Maryland Commission on Indian Affairs. After the opening, Chief Mark Tayac, the 29th-generation hereditary chief of the Piscataway Nation, took the microphone and directed the rest of the powwow's activities. Chief Tayac began by describing what powwows represent: joy, strength and community. Today, powwows show the world that despite generational trauma, historical oppression and systemic inequality, Indigenous culture has survived and is still thriving. Chief Tayac then called the dancers and drummers to begin the ceremony. A group of four drummers provided the music for most of the dances. The dances were of rotating variety: one was a social dance for anyone to join, one was a solo "Fancy War Dance" performed by one young man, one was a dance performed just by women and one was a couples dance. The routines and costumes were eye-catching and elaborate. In addition to the Native American dance performances, there was also an Indigenous Mexican performance by members of the Mexica people. Their ceremony contained dance, drums and a conch-shell trumpet. Indigenous vendors and community programs set up booths surrounding the middle of the event space. Attendees could purchase jewelry, learn about the resources of the Native American LifeLines Urban Indian Health Program or register for the Baltimore American Indian Center's citywide powwow, taking place on Saturday, Nov. 21. The festivities continued after the dance ceremonies ended, with food being served and people walking around socializing. Aparajita Vaid, a first-year graduate student in the School of Education, described the powwow as a great "opportunity to understand more about [Indigenous] culture." She said the highlight of the event was the ceremonial dances. The School of Public Health's Center for Indigenous Health was also instrumental in setting up the powwow. For anyone wanting to enjoy more indigenous art, the center advertised its upcoming event, Returning to Balance: Indigenous Youth, Arts & Healing, an art and music show taking place both at the Johns Hopkins University Bloomberg Center at 555 Pennsylvania Avenue and virtually on Thursday, Nov. 12.

articles.title: A history of Indigenous Peoples' Day and Baltimore
articles.description: On Monday, Oct. 12 the University and the city of Baltimore celebrated Indigenous Peoples' Day. Simultaneously, Maryland and the U.S. federal government celebrated Columbus Day. The name of the second Monday of October has been a national debate for decades. In some states, both names are listed, while other states choose just one. The federal government gives its employees a paid day off for Columbus Day, but some states regard Indigenous Peoples' Day as a "public holiday" without the day off for state government employees. Maryland is unique in that there is both a paid state holiday for Columbus Day and American Indian Heritage Day, the Friday after Thanksgiving. Different groups have differing opinions on Maryland's and Baltimore's choices of days of celebration. In a written interview with The News-Letter, Nina Gover Brooks, the director of the Baltimore American Indian Center (BAIC) shared her perspective on the debate. "Indigenous People's Day should be considered and recognized as a state holiday," she explained. "Although we are excited to hear about the announcement of American Indian Heritage Day, many people feel it makes indigenous people seem like an afterthought…greatly overshadowed by the American celebration of Thanksgiving and Black Friday given the fact that is the Friday after the major holiday," she wrote. The News-Letter also reached out to John Pica, the Baltimore-based President of Italian American Organizations United, who shared his thoughts in an interview with The News-Letter. Pica's response to Baltimore's decision to rename Columbus Day to Indigenous Peoples' Day was generally supportive. "We had no problem with renaming Columbus Day to Italian Heritage Day, but the council wouldn't do that, so Indigenous Peoples Day is fine, and we don't oppose that at all," he said. "In Baltimore City, it really doesn't matter what they do, because it's not recognized as officially changing the holiday. There's still a federal holiday, and there's still a state holiday." To understand these differing perspectives, we must look into Baltimore's complicated history of the holiday. History Baltimore was one of the first cities to celebrate Columbus Day. On Oct. 12, 1792 the Columbus Obelisk was erected in Baltimore, celebrating the 300th anniversary of Columbus' landing. Since then, Baltimore has put up two more statues honoring Columbus, one in Druid Hill Park and one in the appropriately named Columbus Park, adjacent to Baltimore's Little Italy neighborhood. The last one was torn down in 2020. The city's large Italian community, centered around the historic St. Leo's Catholic Church, celebrated the holiday with a parade for 122 years, the longest running Columbus parade in the country. This is much longer than the day has even existed as a federal holiday. Columbus Day was only designated as a federal holiday in 1968, during the Lyndon B. Johnson administration. For centuries, Christopher Columbus was treated as a hero and as the "discoverer of the Americas" by American schools. His journey has been a symbolic source of pride for Italian American communities, who have faced xenophobic discrimination in the history of the U.S. However, through the consistent efforts of both Indigenous and non-Indigenous historians and scholars, the heroic perception of Columbus as a person has shifted. His actions have been critically reexamined, and it is generally agreed that he perpetrated the conquest, enslavement and murder of Indigenous people. Furthermore, his actions, the intentionality of which remains debated, led to the genocide of the Indigenous population of the Americas: it is estimated that 95% of the Indigenous population of the Americas died in the 130 years after 1492. In 1977, not long after Columbus Day's designation as a federal holiday, groups began advocating for its name to be changed. In 1992, Indigenous groups protested national quincentennial Columbus Day celebrations, and states and cities began changing Columbus Day to Indigenous Peoples' Day. Baltimore has a rich and continuous history of Indigenous presence. Baltimore contains part of the ancestral homelands of the Piscataway and Susquehannock peoples. Both tribes still have a presence in the Baltimore community. Chief Mark Tayac, the 29th-generation hereditary chief of the Piscataway Nation, was one of the leaders present at the University's eighth annual powwow. A powwow is a traditional Indigenous American social gathering containing dancing and singing. Baltimore's current Indigenous population also contains thousands of Lumbee and Cherokee people who migrated here during the 1950s and '60s. They mostly settled in East Baltimore, specifically in the Upper Fells Point and Washington Hill neighborhoods. Their neighborhood became nicknamed "The Reservation." Despite much of the community moving outside "The Reservation" in the decades since, the neighborhood is still full of history. Ashley Minner, a Lumbee community artist, has created a public memory walking tour project where one can explore the neighborhood's history. It includes churches (such as the South Broadway Baptist Church), storefronts, restaurants, community centers (such as the BAIC) and murals (such as the Duality of Indigeneity Mural). Baltimore's Indigenous community has been an active force in pushing for the renaming of Columbus Day and for the celebration of Indigenous Peoples' Day. In 2017, Kerry Hawk Lessard, the executive director of Baltimore-based Native American Lifelines and a Shawnee nation member, released a statement in support of changing Columbus Day to Indigenous Peoples' Day. "Rejecting painful reminders of the past and instead embracing the resilience and presence of Native people is an important step in the empowerment and healing of our communities," he wrote. In 2020, Baltimore's City Council passed a bill officially changing the name of Columbus Day to Indigenous Peoples' Day, with the support of the advocacy group Indigenous Strong. However, Gover Brooks says the necessary work in honoring and uplifting Indigenous communities is not complete. "The city of Baltimore does a pretty decent job with celebrating and recognizing Indigenous Peoples' Day," she said. "However, one thing I know that could change to benefit the Indigenous community here is if the city would partner with local Indigenous organizations more often to plan celebrations and/or fundraisers to keep these cultural pillars alive," she wrote. Columbus statue In 2020, the combination of the increasingly critical views of Christopher Columbus and the wave of George Floyd-inspired Black Lives Matter protests culminated in the toppling of one of the historic Columbus statues in Baltimore. On the night of July 4, 2020 a large group of protestors gathered at Columbus Park, which is right by the harbor, and pulled the Columbus statue off its pedestal and dumped it into the water. The toppling had mixed reactions in Maryland and Baltimore. Then-governor Larry Hogan posted a statement supporting civic engagement while discouraging vandalism. "While we welcome peaceful protests and constructive dialogue on whether and how to put certain monuments in context or move them to museums or storage through a legal process, lawlessness, vandalism, and destruction of public property is completely unacceptable," he wrote. "That is the antithesis of democracy and should be condemned by everyone, regardless of their politics. Baltimore City leaders need to regain control of their own streets and immediately start making them safer." Meanwhile, then-City Council President and now Mayor Brandon Scott voiced his support for the removal of the Columbus statue, but not necessarily the protestors' methods. He additionally voiced his support for Baltimore's Italian American community and the city's Indigenous community and stated that he cannot "support Columbus." To understand Baltimore's large Italian American community's reaction to the statue's destruction, The News-Letter asked Pica about his and the community's views on Columbus, Columbus Day and his statue. First, Pica clarified that Baltimore's Italian American and Catholic communities' pride in Columbus is not in the man himself, but rather is symbolic. "It's symbolic of his adventure. It's symbolic of creating an oceanic highway that brought my grandparents here and immigrants all over Europe," he said. "We don't raise a glass to Columbus. We raise a glass to Italy and to Italian American heritage." His view is that the toppling of the Columbus Statue was unfavorable and ineffective. "I don't think it was related to Floyd... It was a bunch of punks between 17 and 25 years old… thinking they were doing something courageous, thinking they were doing something good," he claimed. "In fact, they destroyed a statue that was worth more than a half million dollars. The saddest part of that whole evening was that two dozen Baltimore police officers watched the whole thing and did nothing." What will take the place of the old statue? Well, Baltimore's Italian American community used tow trucks and rope to retrieve the sunken Columbus statue from the Inner Harbor. Then, they hired a sculptor to recreate the statue. However, this replica is not on the old pedestal in Baltimore; instead, it is sitting on display at the White House in Washington, D.C. There are plans for what will take Columbus' place in Baltimore. Pica explained some possible replacement options. "We've now raised over $240,000 for a statue of an Italian immigrant family that will go on the pedestal where Columbus once sat," he said. "We're going to have three brass plaques memorializing the different cultures that live there: the African Americans who lived side by side with the Italians, Jews who lived side by side on the other side of Little Italy and the two Native American tribes that preceded everyone on that land." The new statue is in the works to be completed in the winter of 2027. Hopkins Hopkins preceded Baltimore to renaming Columbus Day as Indigenous Peoples' Day, doing so in 2018. This came after years of gatherings and protests by the University's Indigenous students. On Indigenous Peoples' Day in 2018, the University's Indigenous Students at Hopkins (ISH) group and the Office of Multicultural Affairs hosted their first official powwow celebration, an annual tradition ever since. Despite its official celebration of Indigenous Peoples' Day, Hopkins' commitment to Indigenous studies leaves room to be desired. Hopkins currently does not have an Indigenous studies department or a specific professor or faculty dedicated to studying American Indigenous Studies. To resolve this, students in the Critical Diaspora Studies major have created a working group, one point of advocacy being to hire a tenured faculty member in American Indigenous Studies. Critics argue that without advanced research into or undergraduate-accessible classes about American Indigenous history and culture, Hopkins fails to follow its statement on principles of diversity, equity and inclusion, which emphasizes "diverse identities, perspectives, and experiences." Hopkins also has a very low number of Indigenous students. Hopkins reported that the Class of 2029 has 1.1% of students of American Indian/Alaska Native background and 0.4% of Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander background. Furthermore, the formerly active ISH undergraduate organization seems to be no longer active. Hopkins does have a world-renowned graduate program in Indigenous studies: the Bloomberg School of Public Health's Center for Indigenous Health. Founded in 1991, the Center has served to promote "Indigenous health equity through evidence-based public health programs, education, innovative research, policy advocacy, and the dissemination of proven programs tailored to community needs." While physically based in Washington, D.C., most of the work of the center takes place in actual Indigenous communities across the U.S. and the rest of the world. 80% of the Center's employees are Indigenous, and over 90% of the Center's team members work directly in their communities. For students interested in becoming more involved in Baltimore's Indigenous community, the BAIC has a plethora of resources and events available. Gover Brooks emphasized this point in a statement. "Students can get involved with the BAIC just by reaching out! You can sign up on our website to volunteer or reach out via e-mail or phone and ask us directly for more information. Most of our events are free to the community including our culture class which takes place at the center every Tuesday at 6:00pm-7:30pm. Please do not be a stranger, just show up if you have to & the center is happy to welcome any indigenous person looking to connect. Regardless of the background." The BAIC will be hosting a Native American Heritage Month celebration on Nov. 7, and it will also be hosting its annual Powwow on Nov. 21. Students can also take a short shuttle ride downtown to Little Italy. They can see the site of the old Columbus Statue and then check out some of the great restaurants in the area. "La Scala… it's an Italian family that runs it. The best Italian restaurants are run by families… Benny's is a good restaurant… and Chiapparelli's got great pasta," Pica recommended. Baltimore is a city with a complicated past. It is therefore no surprise that the city's history of Columbus Day and Indigenous Peoples' Day is complex and dynamic, sure to change more in the coming years.

articles.title: GM just did 34,000 years of battery testing in less than a month. Here’s how
articles.description: Developing new EV battery technology takes years of research. General Motors, for example, says it’s put a decade of effort into lithium manganese-rich, or LMR, batteries, which aren’t yet in any of their vehicles on the road. But recently, the automaker says it made a big leap in that work. Using computer modeling, GM was able to virtually test more than 300,000 LMR battery pack configurations, advancing from first concept to formal approval in under a month. That represents more than 300 million CPU hours, which would take a typical computer 34,000 years, while running 24 hours a day, to complete, according to GM. GM is leaning into artificial intelligence and virtual simulations to develop its vehicles. That not only speeds up the time to do testing, per the company, but allows it to test more options, rather than picking the best of just a few configurations. Those 300,000 formulations, for example, looked at different chemical combinations, temperature cycling, and other approaches to creating a battery cell, Sterling Anderson, GM’s chief product officer, told Fast Company. “If we had not had the luxury of some of these tools, we would have had to sample more sparsely from what was possible,” he says. Speeding up vehicle development GM is bringing this AI approach beyond battery testing and into all areas of its vehicle development, with the aim of slashing the time it takes to develop a car in half. Typically, cars are developed within a four- or five-year time frame. That allows a “limited number” of all kinds of tests, Anderson says, from wind tunnel to crash tests. “Now in the virtual world, instead of the X crash test that we could have done, or Y prototypes that could go through, we can run X times 100 and Y times 1000,” he says. GM is also working to advance its autonomous driving capabilities with real-world and virtual testing. Hundreds of data-collection vehicles are currently driving across the country collecting 1 million miles of data a month, while virtually, GM systems drive more than 3 billion simulated miles a day. By cutting vehicle development down to about two years, GM also says it can adapt more quickly to external challenges. Many car makers were counting on Biden-era EV tax credits to help their sales, for example, but then the Trump administration cut those credits. Tariffs, the war in Iran’s effect on gas prices, changing regulations, and uneasy consumer sentiments have all added uncertainty to automakers’ future product lineups, which may have been in development for years. A shorter development cycle “makes you more agile,” Anderson says. LMR batteries in the works GM wants to be the first automaker to deploy LMR batteries, and Anderson says they’re on track to make that happen. LMR batteries can have 33% more energy density than lithium iron phosphate chemistry, and use a higher amount of less-expensive minerals (like manganese) rather than more of the most expensive minerals like cobalt and nickel. That allows them to offer more range—potentially more than 400 miles—at a lower cost and lighter weight. GM is also preparing to roll out its fourth-generation EV platform, which includes not only LMR batteries but a centralized, upgraded computing system, and new electrical work. It will have 30% less wiring than GM’s current EVs and 40% fewer parts in its motors and power electronics, which make it lighter and more efficient. GM and LG Energy Solution are working on these batteries as part of a joint venture called Ultium Cells. They plan to start commercial production of the LMR battery cells in the U.S. by 2028, at the Ultium Cells facility in Spring Hill, Tennessee.

articles.title: Tech-savvy STEM students prone to letting AI do their thinking for them, study shows
articles.description: CORVALLIS, Ore. – University students with traits coveted in STEM fields are also the ones most prone to relying on artificial intelligence to the detriment of their cognitive skills, according to a new study by scientists at Oregon State University. Researchers in OSU’s colleges of Engineering and Liberal Arts offer suggestions for breaking what they call “the self-reinforcing cognitive debt cycle” stemming from routine AI dependence. The study led by computer science graduate student Rudrajit “Rudy” Choudhuri indicates that without corrective action by educators and AI designers, thinking skills will steadily decline amid an illusion of increased efficiency.“Our findings make you rethink what kind of AI literacy is useful after all,” he said. Choudhuri and doctoral advisor Anita Sarma teamed up with Margaret Burnett, distinguished professor of computer science, and Christopher Sanchez, associate professor of psychological science, to analyze survey data from 299 STEM students representing five North American universities. The analysis, published in Information and Software Technology, reveals a feedback loop: The routine use of generative AI serves to weaken students’ intellectual habits, which leads them to lean on AI even more, further diminishing their thinking skills.“The most surprising finding was that the ‘AI-savvy’ ones, who you might think do significantly better in STEM careers, are actually spinning themselves deeper into the AI dependence spiral,” Choudhuri said. “The choices educators and AI designers make now will shape not only what students learn, but how they learn to think.”The researchers note that the “cognitive laziness” associated with an over-reliance on AI is explained at least in part by evolution. Our ancestors who learned the skillful use of intuitive, automatic and low-effort “system 1” thinking were able to outcompete those who overapplied “system 2” thinking, which is deliberate, controlled and effortful.“System 1 is what delivers the rapid answer to 2 + 2 = ? or completes the phrase ‘bread and _____,” Choudhuri said. “System 2 is invoked when you calculate 17 × 24 or evaluate a complex argument. System 2 is lazy. It avoids effort whenever System 1 can provide a plausible solution. It’s what psychologists call the law of least effort, which is a pervasive tendency to accept the path of least cognitive resistance.”Basically, human ancestors who conserved their mental energy for actual threats survived whereas those who performed exhaustive analyses prior to every decision didn’t.“Today we make shopping lists rather than rely on memory, let calculators do our arithmetic and use GPS instead of reading maps,” Sarma added. “Generative AI tools tend to amplify this sort of trend because they deliver fluent, confident support on demand. That means interacting with AI is more about choosing from outputs rather than thinking by doing.”Though choosing instead of thinking can create a compelling sense of progress via time savings, they said, it’s problematic for learning. That’s particularly true in STEM education, where students need “desirable difficulties” – slow, painstaking cognitive work that builds intuition and transferable skills. In the survey, students who trusted and routinely used generative AI reported significantly lower cognitive engagement.“The types of skills that students are farming out to AI actually put them in a hole when it comes to developing skills that are genuinely needed,” Sanchez said. “In short, they are not using AI as an assistant but as more of a substitute for actually engaging with learning a topic.”The scientists suggest some ways for students to build these cognitive skills, including:Increasing the intrinsic reward of cognitive engagement by designing coursework as opportunities for exploration through storytelling, game playing or puzzle solving. Alternating between AI-assisted and independent work. For example, students might first problem solve with help from AI, then be required to independently critique, debug/repair, verify and adapt that contribution to their project requirements without AI during a supervised lab. Combining these approaches with in-class assessments and/or collaborative/group activities to further reinforce engagement by leveraging social accountability. Designing generative AI systems as “bicycles for the mind.” Bikes amplify physical efficiency while requiring the rider’s active control; designed as mind-bicycles, AI would amplify cognition via critique, counter argument and provocation while keeping humans responsible for exploration, steering and judgment.“Absent intervention, STEM education runs the risk of cultivating a generation of students unwilling and/or unable to exercise their capacity for reflection, understanding and critical thinking,” Burnett said. “If routine reliance on AI changes students’ willingness to engage in effortful thinking, many may enter professional life without having developed the intellectual habits that earlier generations gained through practice.”The USDA National Institute of Food and Agriculture and the National Science Foundation supported this study.

articles.description: Good growth: Innovate Cambridge Summit 2026 Sarah Fell Thu, 10/22/2026 - 09:56 New analysis from Cambridge Innovation Capital (CIC), published ahead of the Summit, showed the average equity raised per deal across both life sciences and deep tech has increased five-fold in the last decade, with Cambridge-based early-stage companies having raised £9.1 billion in that period. Taking leadership in innovation Professor Deborah Prentice, Vice-Chancellor of the University of Cambridge reflected on what makes Cambridge such a thriving innovation economy and the importance of taking a proactive and global leadership role in driving innovation that works for everyone: “There are three ways in which Cambridge takes leadership: through research excellence, by acting as one ecosystem and through our partnerships with other places and organisations.” These themes were echoed by speakers throughout the day, including Mayor Paul Bristow, Peter Freeman (Chair of the Greater Cambridge Development Corporation) and Roland Sinker (Chair of the Inclusive Innovation and Growth Review, University of Cambridge) with a recurring focus on breakthrough research, ambitious partnerships and a shared sense of purpose across the ecosystem. Strengthening the life sciences ecosystem Following GSK’s recent announcement that it will be moving its R&D headquarters to Cambridge in 2029, Chief Scientific Officer, Tony Wood spoke about the increasing need for collaboration in the life sciences and that by moving to Cambridge GSK will be able to create more opportunities to achieve breakthroughs in drug discovery and patient care. Global ambitions for quantum computing John Aston, Pro-Vice-Chancellor for Research at the University of Cambridge led a discussion considering the UK’s global leadership role in spearheading the development and application of quantum computing. The University’s partnership with IonQ, which next year will bring the UK’s first commercial scale quantum computer to Cambridge, combined with the University’s research strengths in both quantum and its potential applications, underpinned by the ecosystem’s strength in supporting commercialisation, means that Cambridge is uniquely placed to play a national – and global - leadership role. City partnerships: Manchester and Cambridge Faye Holland (Director, Cambridge x Manchester Partnership) described the increasing success of the partnership between Cambridge and Manchester in combining the regions’ complementary strengths to increase the UK’s global competitiveness. The pioneering model for this cross-city approach is now being championed by government and adopted by other city partnerships across the UK. Keeping jobs and know-how in the UK How to create the right conditions for start-ups to grow, scale and stay in the UK was explored, and the creation of a new task force announced by Pascal Levensohn (Chair of Cambridge Innovation Hub Global Advisory Board) to take forward a new approach (outlined in a white paper published ahead of the Summit) to keeping a company’s footprint in the UK even if it is acquired internationally. The Summit also heard from some of Cambridge’s most successful start-ups including Nyobolt and T-Therapeutics (both of which spun out of the University with support from Cambridge Enterprise) as well as Pragmatic Semiconductors, Cambridge Aerospace and CuspAI. Widening opportunities Ensuring that innovation-led growth benefits everyone who lives and works in Cambridge and the wider region was a central and recurring theme. Included, a new initiative to create more opportunities for young people in Greater Cambridge was announced at the Summit, with organisations present asked to contribute opportunities such as workplace visits, work experience and mentoring. Accelerating the energy transition In a parallel session, leaders from across the Cambridge cleantech ecosystem discussed accelerating the UK's clean energy transition. Hosted by DESNZ, Innovate Cambridge and Cambridge Zero, and chaired by Professor Emily Shuckburgh, Chief Scientific Adviser at DESNZ, the session brought together experts from industry, investment, academia and government. Discussions explored the opportunities and barriers to scaling cleantech innovation and commercialisation, alongside the role that innovation clusters such as Cambridge can play in addressing national clean energy challenges. articles.title: Taiwan issues warnings as Typhoon Champi nears
articles.description: A powerful typhoon headed toward Taiwan on Thursday, triggering the cancellation of dozens of flights and prompting warnings for locals to prepare for heavy rain, strong winds and giant waves.
